newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish government scores tax victory.
newsitem.headline: Polish government scores tax victory.

text.p: Poland's government won a qualified victory in the Senate over its 1997 budget plans on Thursday, when the upper house rejected proposals for a deep cut in the personal income tax for the most needy next year.

The Senate scrapped the lower house's motion to change tax levels to 17, 20, 33 and 45 percent in 1997, which the finance ministry said would throw Poland's finances into disarray, from this year's 21, 33 and 45 percent. @

In a 44 to 33 vote with nine abstentions, the upper house approved a tax scale of 20, 32, and 44 percent and Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko welcomed the decision even though it differed from the government's own proposals.
The vote coincided with the launch of a parliamentary debate on the 1997 national budget, which must be approved by the lower house by January 28.
"The Senate's decision is sensible and compatible with solutions proposed by the government," Kolodko told reporters.
He had earlier proposed to cut tax levels to 20, 31 and 43 percent next year. @
President Aleksander Kwasniewski, who has suggested he would veto the radical tax cut, also supported the Senate's tax decision, his press office told Reuters.

Both the government's and senate's tax scales would maintain next year's budget deficit at this year's planned level of 2.8 percent of gross domestic product, while increasing real-term spending and revenues by 2.3 percent and 2.8 percent respectively. @

The government budget draft assumes that year-on-year inflation would be cut to 13 percent in December next year from 17.8 percent expected in 1996 and that GDP will continue to grow at 5.5 percent, reaching 430 billion zlotys.

Central bank president Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz said on Thursday that any deficit higher than 2.4 percent of GDP would require a more restrictive monetary policy next year if government macroeconomic targets are to be met. @

The lower house, expected to give the tax bill a final reading next week, may still reinstate its four-bracket tax scale, which Kolodko said would entail either a radical cut in spending or boosting the budget gap beyond reasonable limits.
But this appeared unlikely despite disagreements on the issue in the ruling coalition of ex-communists and a Peasant party.

Although the Peasants strongly back a deep tax cut for the poorest in society, the larger ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance and the biggest opposition party, the Union for Freedom, declared support for the Senate's tax proposal. @
"I confirm that the Union (for Freedom) will vote in favour of this scale," its chairman Leszek Balcerowicz told a news conference.

Some analysts say the Peasants, the less liberal partner in the coalition, insist on lowering taxes for the numerous members of the lowest income group to boost their chances in parliamentary elections, due late next year.
